details: Graphite combustion reactions: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g); ΔH = -393.5 kJ/mol (complete combustion); C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g); ΔH = -110.5 kJ/mol (incomplete combustion; Boudouard reaction); CO + ½O₂ → CO₂; ΔH = -283 kJ/mol; Boudouard reaction (above 700°C): CO₂ + C → 2CO (endothermic +172.5 kJ/mol); above ~700°C: Boudouard equilibrium shifts to CO production; graphite ignition temperature: nuclear grade graphite: 700-900°C (purity grade affects ignition); Windscale 1957: graphite fire at similar temperature (graphite pile; air-cooled; Wigner energy release → ignition; first nuclear graphite fire); RBMK graphite: 1700 tonnes; reactor-grade (high purity; <5 ppm boron equivalent; minimizes neutron absorption); graphite density: 1.7 g/cm³ (nuclear grade vs 2.26 theoretical); graphite in Chernobyl fire: exposed when reactor vessel destroyed → contact with air (oxygen) → ignition > 700°C from decay heat + Zr-water reaction heat
chernobyl_application: RBMK graphite fire 1986: ignition April 26 01:23:47 (within 3s of explosion); sustained burn: April 26 to May 9 1986 = 14 days; temperature: 1200-1700°C (estimated from satellite thermal imaging and material analysis); CO₂ and CO plume rose with hot gases to 1-2 km altitude (plume height); graphite combustion heat: 1700t × 10% burned × 394 kJ/mol × 1000/(12 g/mol) = 56,000 GJ (estimate for partial combustion); equivalent to 56 GWh thermal; sustained fire = sustained aerosol generation = reason for multi-phase release profile over 14 days; graphite combustion products: CO₂ + CO + graphite aerosols (PAH, soot) + radionuclide aerosols (Cs-137 vapor condensed onto combustion particles)
source: Cherepnin 1966 (graphite properties); source_term_daily_release_REAL.csv; rbmk_thermal_hydraulics_REAL.csv; Windscale_1957 comparison

details: Fire suppression strategy: initial misunderstanding: April 26-27: MVD firefighters attacked roof fires (not reactor); direct water application to roof bitumen fires successfully extinguished roof blazes; PROBLEM: reactor graphite fire below = no water could be applied directly (steam explosion risk); helicopters: began dropping materials April 27; total materials: ~5100 tonnes: sand (2040t; 40%): smother oxygen access; boron carbide B₄C (40t; 0.8%): neutron absorber (but reactor already subcritical); clay (1275t; 25%): smother + bind; lead (650t; 13%): absorb gamma + melt to seal (lead melts 327°C; vaporizes 1749°C; at 1650°C reactor temp → significant lead vaporization); dolomite (510t; 10%; CaMg(CO₃)₂): releases CO₂ at high temperature (endothermic decomposition → CO₂ → may suppress fire); effect of materials: partially sealed core → temporarily reduced air access → fire reduced May 6-7; then second peak May 6-8 (possible disturbance of debris)
chernobyl_application: Fire outcome: graphite fire extinguished naturally May 9-10 1986; mechanism: oxygen depletion in sealed core cavity; NOT effectively suppressed by helicopter drops; evidence: release rate plots (source_term_daily_release_REAL.csv) show: Day 1-2 high; Day 3-7 lower; Day 8-10 second peak; Day 10 abrupt stop = fire out; helicopter materials effect disputed; 1700 tonnes graphite: ~10-15% burned (~170-250t); remaining graphite: incorporated into corium/FCM structures; graphite combustion = primary mechanism for aerosolizing fission products (Cs volatile at 670°C; temperature >> volatilization threshold; swept into plume by fire convection)
source: Pazukhin 1994 Radiochimica Acta 26:37-47; source_term_daily_release_REAL.csv; atmospheric_aerosol_physics_REAL.csv; corium_fcm_physics_REAL.csv

details: Graphite fire convective column: fire thermal power peak: estimated 1-4 GW (day 1-2); convective column rise: buoyant plume equation h = 1.6 × F^(1/4) × u^(-3/4) where F = buoyancy flux (m⁴/s³); u = wind speed; at F = 10⁷ m⁴/s³ (1GW thermal) and u=3 m/s: h_rise ≈ 1200m; actual effective plume height: 1000-2000m (lofted above boundary layer mixing height ~500m); consequence: material lofted above mixing layer → transported thousands of km without significant deposition en route; mixing layer height at Pripyat April 26: ~800-1200m (daytime clear sky); April 27 (night): ~200-400m; explains why: close areas (Pripyat) had lower initial deposition than expected (plume height above city) but distant areas (Scandinavia) received measurable activity within 36-48 hours; Cs-137 aerosol AMAD 0.3-1 µm from fire condensation → long atmospheric residence
chernobyl_application: Fire-associated radionuclide volatilization: temperatures > volatilization points: Cs (670°C; highly volatile); Te (990°C; volatile); I₂ (184°C; volatile); Sb (630°C; volatile); Mo (4639°C; refractory); Ru (>4000°C; refractory; but RuO₄ volatile above 1000°C → Ru-106 release mechanism); Ba-140 (1640°C; partially volatile at fire temperature); Pu: non-volatile below 3232°C but dispersed as fuel particle fragments; graphite fire at 1200-1700°C volatilizes Cs, I, Te completely; releases significant Ba/Ru as oxide aerosols; Pu/Am/Ce/Zr/Nb remain as refractory fuel particles near NPP

details: Two distinct fire types April 26: (1) Turbine hall roof (bitumen/tar): conventional fire; effectively extinguished by firefighters within 2-3 hours; external gamma from roof proximity + some smoke inhalation of aerosol; (2) Reactor graphite fire: underground/open-top; not accessible to conventional firefighting; firefighters on reactor roof exposed to: direct beta/gamma from open core; inhalation of fuel aerosols from convective plume; no protective equipment suitable for this radiation environment; fire chief Pravik (1st watch) on Unit 4 reactor roof: dose estimated 5-6 Gy; fire chief Kibenok (2nd watch): similar; both died within 2 weeks; firefighter dose-response: 28 deaths from ARS out of 134 ARS cases; dose threshold for ARS: >0.7 Gy; threshold for lethality without treatment: ~3.5 Gy; firefighters who stayed on roof > 10 minutes: essentially all received lethal doses without aggressive treatment
chernobyl_application: Dose pathway for firefighters: (1) External gamma (dominant): open core geometry → dose rate ~1000-15,000 R/hr at roof level; 10-minute exposure at 5000 R/hr = 50 Gy = extreme; distance modifies: 10m from edge = factor 100 reduction = 50 Gy/hr; 50m = 0.5 Gy/hr = 1 hr to lethal dose; (2) Beta skin dose: clothing provided partial protection but beta burns still occurred (boots; face; bare arms); (3) Inhalation: fuel aerosols + volatile fission products in plume; firefighters reported 'chemical taste in mouth' = I-131 inhalation = absorption in thyroid; (4) No ingestion pathway (fire scene); see ars_cases_REAL.csv for individual case details

details: Windscale Pile 1 fire comparison (October 8-12 1957; Cumbria UK): reactor design: air-cooled open-cycle graphite pile (weapon-grade Pu production); accident cause: Wigner energy release (stored energy in crystalline graphite lattice from radiation damage) → graphite overheated → bitumen cartridge filter ignition → fire; fire suppression: carbon dioxide first (failed); WATER applied to graphite (risk: steam/hydrogen; but succeeded); extinguished after 16 hours by flooding; release: ~740 TBq I-131; ~46 TBq Cs-137; ~8 TBq other; contamination: 2 million liters milk banned (70km radius); I-131 detected across Europe; no evacuation; INES 5 retroactively assigned; deaths: 240-1000 long-term cancer estimates (controversial); comparison to Chernobyl: Windscale = 740 TBq I-131 vs Chernobyl = 1760 TBq I-131 (Chernobyl 2.4× Windscale); Windscale Cs-137 = 46 TBq vs Chernobyl = 85,000 TBq (Chernobyl 1850× Windscale for Cs-137)
chernobyl_application: Windscale lessons for Chernobyl: (1) Graphite fire can be suppressed with water despite initial risk assessment; (2) Wigner energy = known graphite hazard; RBMK graphite: annealing cycle maintained to prevent Wigner energy buildup (RBMK graphite kept hot continuously unlike Windscale air-cooled design); therefore RBMK fire cause was NOT Wigner energy (was reactor excursion + Zr-water); (3) Windscale classified for 30yr (1987 release of Penney Report); Chernobyl = continuation of pattern that nuclear information suppression fails when radiation reaches other countries; Wigner energy not a concern for modern graphite-moderated reactors (RBMK, HTR) which maintain operating temperature

details: Correlation of graphite fire phases with source term release phases (source_term_daily_release_REAL.csv): Phase 1 (Apr 26 01:23-end): prompt release from explosion; 14% fuel inventory noble gases; 20% iodine; volatile fission products; fuel particles; graphite fire begins simultaneously; Phase 2 (Apr 27-28): helicopter operations begin; moderate fire; first plume to Scandinavia; Phase 3 (Apr 29-May 1): fire partially suppressed by helicopter materials; lower release rate; Phase 4 (May 2-4): fire resurging; boron + clay ineffective; Phase 5 (May 5-8): second peak release (1700-2000°C core temperature based on I-129m/Cs ratio analysis); coincides with melting of remaining fuel; deepest combustion reaching most volatile-rich fuel segments; Phase 6 (May 9-10): rapid decline; fire extinguished naturally (O₂ depletion); release essentially zero May 10+
chernobyl_application: Temperature proxy: Cs-137/I-131 ratio in air samples at monitoring stations shows temperature-dependent shifts; higher T → higher Cs/I (Cs more volatile at high T); Chernobyl sampling data shows temperature peak of May 6-8 = ~1700-2000°C consistent with deepest core combustion; May 9 temperature drop = fire extinguishment; IAEA INSAG-7: temperature evidence confirms two-phase fire (initial rapid cooling from water flooding, then second heating); 14-day duration unprecedented in nuclear accident history; closest comparison: Windscale (16 hours); Chernobyl 20× longer graphite fire duration

details: Smoke aerosol from graphite fire: two aerosol populations: (1) Fresh combustion aerosols (carbon soot): 0.1-0.5 µm primary particles; 0.3-1 µm after coagulation; radionuclides (Cs-137; I-131) condense onto soot particle surfaces as they cool below volatilization temperature; (2) Fuel particles: 4-150 µm uranium oxide fragments propelled by explosion; settle within 10 km; aerosol optical properties: graphite soot = strong light absorber (mass absorption cross-section 10 m²/g); smoke visible from satellite imagery; fire visible from Pripyat; smoke density estimated from meteorological records and AVHRR satellite imagery; aerosol composition at distances >100km: almost purely CsOH/Cs₂SO₄ condensation aerosols (fuel particles fully settled); at 30km: mixed population; volatile Cs-137 at 100-1000km = primary thyroid/WB dose source
chernobyl_application: Aerosol toxicology: graphite + radionuclide aerosol mixture; graphite particles (PM2.5): lung retention; radionuclide attached → lung dose from fuel aerosols; I-131 inhalation → thyroid absorption regardless of particle attachment (NIS transports dissolved iodine); near-field (10-30km): fuel particle inhalation → lung dose (Pu-238/239/240 alpha dose); far-field (>100km): condensation aerosols → Cs-137 lung dose (less critical than external gamma from deposition); ICRP 66 breathing rate adult = 1.2 m³/hr; outdoor exposure 24hr at 10 Bq/m³ Cs-137 = 288 Bq inhaled; committed lung dose = 288 × 1.4×10⁻⁸ Sv/Bq = 4 µSv (negligible vs external gamma)

details: Current (2026) fire risk in CEZ: annual wildfire risk in Red Forest and CEZ: 3-5 significant fire events per decade (based on 1992-2022 history); 2020: largest post-accident wildfire (11,500 ha; 630 GBq Cs-137 atmospheric release); see wildfire_resuspension_REAL.csv; 2022: Russian military activities increased fire risk (disrupted suppression; burned ammunition); DAZV maintains 24/7 fire watch towers; firebreaks constructed; surface contamination fuel (pine needle litter) most dangerous; dose to firefighters in CEZ wildfire: ~0.01-0.1 mSv per hour in smoke plume at fire front; EURDEP monitoring: Cs-137 above baseline detected during 2020 fire but well below notification threshold; current atmospheric Cs-137 from resuspension (2026): 0.001-0.01 Bq/m³ normal → 10-1000 Bq/m³ in dense smoke from active CEZ fire (1000x increase; still 20-200x below occupational air limit 20,000 Bq/m³)
chernobyl_application: 2026 fire risk amplification factors: (1) Climate change: longer dry season; higher fire danger; (2) War: disrupted infrastructure; unexploded ordnance; (3) Vegetation overgrowth: 40 years of unmanaged forest = high fuel load; (4) Am-241 increasing (alpha emitter in soil → higher energy transfer to soil/litter than Cs-137 gamma); MITIGATION: firebreak network; early detection; Ukraine State Emergency Service (DSNS) response teams; Cs-137 fixed in soil aged 40yr (K_p~10⁻⁹) = wildfire mobilizes SURFACE Cs-137 only (~0.5cm top layer); deep Cs-137 not affected; hence 2020 release = 630 GBq vs total inventory 85,000 TBq = 0.0007% mobilized
